title: Estimating pollutant dispersion based on reconstructed mean flow field in a two-dimensional street canyon using two-step physics-informed neural networks
abstract: Urban environments exhibit complex physical phenomena involving multiple interacting and imbalanced variables, making high-resolution measurements challenging and expensive. This study aimed to reduce the measurement demand while accurately estimating the mean flow and pollutant concentration fields using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). To improve the robustness of and mitigate the difficulties faced by PINNs when handling imbalanced outputs, this article proposes a two-step framework in which the airflow and pollutant dispersion within a two-dimensional street canyon are trained separately. In the first step, a PINN reconstructs the mean flow field from sparse velocity data derived from a large eddy simulation and simultaneously estimates the eddy viscosity. In the second step, these results are imposed as fixed fields in the advection–diffusion equation, enabling estimation of the pollutant dispersion from a ground-level line source. By leveraging the accurately reconstructed flow field, the second-step PINN achieves reliable reconstruction of the mean concentration field and turbulent diffusivity. Incorporating the eddy viscosity as additional physical information not only reduces the training cost and improves the accuracy, but also substantially reduces the data requirements. The eddy viscosity data ensure system closure, enabling physics-driven concentration field estimation even in the absence of concentration measurements. Furthermore, a comparison of the optimization strategies shows that the L-BFGS is more effective than Adam because of its second-order characteristics, facilitating convergence in ill-conditioned residual loss landscapes. Overall, the proposed method demonstrates the strong capability of PINNs to handle multiple outputs with imbalanced scaling in urban environments, highlighting their potential for broader applications.

title: Ten questions on digital twins of buildings for transforming building operations
abstract: Buildings are becoming ever more complex to manage during operations, driven by increasing dynamics in energy demand, intermittent on-site power generation, and distributed energy resources, compounded by variable grid pricing signals and the rising threat of extreme weather events causing large-scale power outages. To achieve optimal performance in energy efficiency, demand flexibility, energy resilience, and occupant comfort, new methods and tools are essential for transforming design and operations across a building’s entire life cycle. Digital Twins (DTs), enabled by recent advances in ubiquitous sensing, big data, cloud computing, and AI, offer a transformative approach to creating a real-time, bi-directional digital counterpart of a physical building. This paper presents ten critical questions highlighting the most foundational issues underpinning the successful deployment of digital twins of buildings. The questions are holistically structured around three core themes to provoke significant research and accelerate adoption. The paper first examines the Users and Business aspects, including use cases, stakeholder alignment, business models, and governance structures. It then dives into the Technology foundation, addressing key components, layered software architectures, data integration, semantic interoperability, and the critical issues of cybersecurity and privacy. Finally, it explores Application aspects, such as the role of AI, performance metrics and standards, and the current landscape of software tools. DT technology is still in the early stage of adoption in buildings despite successful pilot applications in preventive maintenance, FDD, and advanced controls to optimize building performance. Several barriers need to be addressed to scale up DT technology in buildings, including high development and maintenance costs, the lack of data-rich infrastructure in buildings, and a shortage of skilled workforce.

title: Field-informed reinforcement learning for multi-objective indoor air quality control in naturally ventilated buildings
abstract: Indoor air quality (IAQ) control in naturally ventilated buildings involves a trade-off between ventilation-driven carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) reduction and particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) infiltration from outdoor environments. This study proposes a physically consistent control framework integrating a physics-informed neural network (PINN) surrogate environment with deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for multi-objective IAQ management under stochastic field conditions. The surrogate environment was constructed from long-term measurements in an occupied office, capturing site-specific pollutant dynamics, occupant behavior, and meteorological conditions. A DRL agent then derived Pareto-optimal policies coordinating natural ventilation and air purification under practical constraints. Multi-seed uncertainty analysis evaluated policy robustness, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) interpreted decision mechanisms. During a 30-day validation period, Pareto policies outperformed measured operation and rule-based baselines. The ventilation-oriented policy eliminated CO 2 violations and reduced mean CO 2 from 776 to 619 ppm, while the purification-oriented policy reduced PM 2.5 violations from 1063 to 83 and mean PM 2.5 from 17.1 to 6.3 µ g/m 3 . Simple baselines remained constrained by the CO 2 –PM 2.5 trade-off: ventilation-only control still produced 902 PM 2.5 violations, whereas rule-based CO 2 –PM 2.5 control produced 495 CO 2 and 267 PM 2.5 violations. In contrast, the intermediate RL-derived Policy 14 achieved 70 CO 2 and 152 PM 2.5 violations. These results demonstrate that physically informed, data-driven control can bridge simulation-based optimization and real-world building operation, providing an interpretable decision-support framework for IAQ management. Its scalability should be interpreted at the methodological-workflow level rather than as direct transferability of the quantitative results or calibrated model parameters.

title: Healthy and energy-efficient building retrofits: A systematic review of CFD, digital twins, and occupant-centred intelligence
abstract: Building retrofits are essential for reducing carbon emissions, improving energy efficiency, and upgrading ageing building stocks. However, interventions such as insulation, airtightness improvement, glazing replacement, and HVAC modernisation can also modify airflow, pollutant transport, thermal comfort, moisture balance, overheating risk, and occupant health. This systematic review examines the role of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), Digital Twins (DTs), occupant behaviour modelling, and machine learning in supporting intelligent, health-centred retrofit strategies. Using a PRISMA-informed methodology, studies applying CFD, DTs, or hybrid approaches to retrofit performance assessment were synthesised. The findings show that conventional energy models are useful for estimating annual energy demand but often fail to capture local airflow patterns, contaminant hotspots, thermal stratification, ventilation effectiveness, and occupant exposure risks. CFD provides detailed insight into airflow, heat transfer, pollutant dispersion, moisture transport, ventilation performance, and airborne infection transmission. Occupant behaviour, including walking, window opening, door use, and occupancy schedules, strongly influences airflow and contaminant pathways, especially in airtight retrofitted buildings. DTs further enhance retrofit assessment by integrating sensor data, predictive simulation, and adaptive control for continuous performance optimisation. Machine learning methods are increasingly used to accelerate CFD predictions, reconstruct indoor environmental fields, and support near-real-time decision-making. Although retrofits can improve winter comfort and reduce heating demand, they may also increase overheating, CO₂ concentrations, VOC accumulation, moisture-related problems, and infection vulnerability when ventilation is inadequate. To address these trade-offs, this review proposes a Retrofit Suitability Index (RSI) integrating energy efficiency, indoor air quality, thermal comfort, health protection, affordability, and user acceptance for healthier, resilient, occupant-centred retrofits.

title: Multi-objective optimization and decision-making in building retrofits: A systematic review of frameworks, trends, and research gaps
abstract: In this study, a systematic literature review is presented on optimization-based building retrofits, with an emphasis on how recent studies structure and use decision-support frameworks. The reviewed studies, published between 2020 and 2026, were classified according to the following criteria: retrofit strategies, objective functions, optimization algorithms, computational tools, climatic contexts, and the integration of Sensitivity Analysis (SA), Machine Learning (ML), Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO), and Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM). The findings show that envelope-related measures, including insulation, window, airtightness, and shading upgrades, remain the most frequently optimized strategies, followed by HVAC improvements and renewable energy integration. The dominant GA-based algorithm is NSGA-II due to its robustness in handling nonlinear, simulation-coupled, and conflicting objectives. However, the primary contribution of this review lies in identifying the fragmented but emerging integration of optimization, SA, ML, and decision-making frameworks. Recent studies have increasingly combined SA for parameter prioritization, ML for surrogate prediction and computational acceleration, MOO for Pareto-front generation, and MCDM for final solution ranking. Despite this progress, integration remains limited by insufficient surrogate-model validation, inconsistent reporting of computational costs, and inadequate assessment of uncertainty effects on Pareto-front accuracy and decision rankings. Economic and life-cycle carbon assessments also remain simplified through the use of static energy prices, fixed emission factors, and inconsistent LCA boundaries. Climatic analysis indicates a dominant focus on cold and multiple or mixed climatic contexts, whereas future climate scenarios remain insufficiently incorporated into the retrofit planning process. The most important gaps in optimization and decision-making frameworks for building retrofits include dynamic carbon and cost modeling, embodied carbon assessment, uncertainty quantification, future climate resilience, and stakeholder-informed decision-making. This review highlights the need for transparent, data-driven, and integrated assessment frameworks to support both resilient and implementable retrofit decisions.

GFNO: A generalized Fourier neural operator framework for wind flow field reconstruction from sparse observations
abstract: This study proposes the Generalized Fourier Neural Operator (GFNO), a modular framework for reconstructing high-resolution wind fields from sparse sensor observations. GFNO decouples sparse flow reconstruction into an embedding stage that transforms irregular observations into latent grid representations and a Fourier-based operator stage that reconstructs the full flow field.The framework systematically combines four representative embeddings with three Fourier kernels under a unified physics-informed objective. GFNO is evaluated on two complementary datasets, including Dataset I containing 2,000 transient flow snapshots under fixed sensor locations and Dataset II containing 3,360 mean flow fields with varying building layouts, inflow directions under various sensor placements.Results reveal that the optimal embedding strategy depends strongly on dataset characteristics. For Dataset I, multilayer perceptron (MLP) embeddings outperform alternatives because geometric information provides no additional discriminative signal under fixed configurations. In contrast, for Dataset II with varying layouts and sensor placements, graph neural network (GNN) embeddings consistently achieve best performance, highlighting the importance of geometric priors in cross-configuration reconstruction.Across all datasets, U-Net-augmented FNO (U-FNO) consistently delivers best performance, indicating the importance of recovering localized flow structures in sparse reconstruction. Sensor counts from 4 to 32 are systematically investigated, revealing that reconstruction accuracy in Dataset I saturates beyond 16 sensors, whereas GNN-based models in Dataset II maintain near-saturated accuracy with as few as four sensors.Complementary out-of-distribution evaluations assess robustness under unseen inflow conditions and limited training data. The proposed framework provides an efficient data-driven evaluation tool for urban flow reconstruction under complex interference configurations.

title: Strategic decarbonisation of Norwegian non-residential buildings: life-cycle, energy and circularity evidence with Danish and German comparators
abstract: Public evidence on low-carbon non-residential buildings is expanding, yet it remains fragmented across life-cycle assessment (LCA), operational energy, reuse, recycling, transport, design for disassembly and digital documentation. An auditable synthesis is developed for six Norwegian flagship projects and their interpretation against selected Danish and German policy, certification and practice comparators. The reframed scope is Norway-centred, with Denmark and Germany used as contextual comparators rather than as equal statistical samples. The method comprised a review of 156 sources, including 84 peer-reviewed journal and conference papers, together with structured case selection, module-based LCA coding, energy-performance interpretation, circularity assessment and ordinal evidence-visibility scoring. The Norwegian cases are Powerhouse Kjørbo, Powerhouse Brattørkaia, Kristian Augusts gate 13, HasleTre, Zero Emission Buildings (ZEB) Laboratory and Ruseløkka School. Danish and German comparators include Green Solution House 2.0, EDGE Südkreuz Berlin, Alnatura Campus Darmstadt and the wider Danish and German regulatory and certification systems. The resulting synthesis is primarily qualitative, as only Powerhouse Kjørbo and Ruseløkka School provide open module-or category-level carbon indicators, and these indicators use different boundaries and reporting categories. A key cross-case insight is that sustainability labels and pilot status do not guarantee reproducibility: underlying quantities, product-to-EPD mappings, transport assumptions and post-occupancy data are often restricted by ownership, confidentiality, fragmented responsibility or communication-oriented reporting. The strongest documented strategies are combinations of retention or material efficiency, verified low-carbon products, reuse, recycled content, short logistics, reversible connections, material passports, low operational demand and renewable energy. Reported indicators include 70% greenhouse-gas reduction and almost 80% material reuse at Kristian Augusts gate 13, about 60% lower emissions reported for HasleTre, about 485,000 kWh yr -1 photovoltaic generation at Powerhouse Brattørkaia and about 60–61% total greenhouse-gas reduction in the as-built Ruseløkka School climate account. AI-supported BIM-to-LCA matching, early carbon prediction, energy surrogate modelling and circular logistics are discussed as an auditable decision-support layer derived from the wider literature, rather than as workflows already implemented in the nine cases.

title: Deep learning based determination of thermal-optical and light transmission properties of complex fenestration systems for high throughput applications
abstract: Physically detailed thermal–optical models for complex fenestration systems (CFSs) are computationally expensive, particularly when evaluating glazing and shading systems with strong angular dependence. This limits the practical use of ISO 15099-based calculations in large-scale design exploration, optimisation, and building-performance simulation workflows. This study investigates whether a physics-informed neural surrogate can reproduce ISO 15099-derived thermal-optical response fields while retaining sufficient fidelity for building-scale simulation. A TabNet-based surrogate was developed using 5,760 ISO 15099-compliant façade configurations and trained to predict 145-dimensional SHGC distributions together with directional-hemispherical visible transmittance. Results show that the surrogate reconstructs these high-dimensional response fields with substantially lower error than an interpolation-based k-nearest-neighbour benchmark, reducing SHGC RMSE from 0.0372 to 0.0074 and visible-transmittance RMSE from 0.0423 to 0.0075. Relative to deterministic ISO 15099 calculations, evaluation time decreases from 57.78 s to 2.25 × 10⁻⁴ s per façade configuration. Learning-curve analysis indicates stable convergence, limited evidence of overfitting, and robust performance across different training-data fractions and random initialisations. An ablation study further demonstrates that physics-informed weighting of physically sensitive and energetically relevant angular regions improves prediction accuracy compared with a conventional loss formulation. To assess downstream applicability, surrogate-predicted SHGC fields were propagated into annual TRNSYS simulations for Stuttgart and Doha climates. For both locations, more than 92% of configurations remained within 5% deviation of ISO 15099 reference results and more than 98% remained within 10%, indicating that local prediction errors are largely attenuated at building scale. The results demonstrate that physics-informed surrogate modelling can extend detailed fenestration analysis to high-throughput façade design, optimisation, and building-performance simulation workflows.

Machine learning surrogate models for moisture-risk prediction in cross-laminated timber wall assemblies under wind-driven rain leakage
abstract: Numerical hygrothermal simulations are widely used to assess the moisture durability of mass timber envelopes, but their computational cost limits their use in large-scale probabilistic assessments. Machine learning surrogate models offer a faster alternative, yet their reliability for predicting the nonlinear moisture response of cross-laminated timber (CLT) wall assemblies under wind-driven rain (WDR) leakage remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates Random Forest (RF), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models for predicting temperature, relative humidity (RH), and moisture content (MC) at the exterior surface of CLT panels. The models were trained and tested using DELPHIN-generated data covering four CLT wall configurations, four orientations, 17 Canadian climates, and two moisture-loading scenarios: no leakage and 1% WDR leakage applied to the CLT surface. Under no-leakage conditions, all models predicted temperature accurately, with R 2 values greater than 0.99. For RH and MC, LSTM and CNN outperformed RF, while LSTM achieved high accuracy with shorter training time. Under WDR leakage, LSTM and CNN reproduced the main moisture response trends for assemblies with vapor-permeable exterior insulation. However, prediction accuracy decreased substantially for assemblies with vapor-impermeable exterior insulation, where leakage caused localized water retention, high moisture accumulation, and delayed drying. In these cases, MC predictions showed R 2 values below 0.60. The results indicate that LSTM-based surrogate models can support efficient simulation-based hygrothermal assessment of CLT wall assemblies under normal moisture loading and WDR-leakage conditions with sufficient drying potential, but physics-informed models are needed for restricted-drying conditions dominated by liquid-water transport and moisture storage.

title: Vertical wind profiles and urban morphology effects on nocturnal urban heat islands from Doppler LiDAR observations and machine learning
abstract: Nocturnal urban heat islands (UHI) in high density cities are influenced by local morphology and vertical atmospheric structure. Most UHI assessments have relied on near-surface measurements and the interaction between vertical wind profiles and heterogeneous urban morphology is insufficiently explored. This study investigates how vertical wind pattern is associated with nocturnal UHI during summer months in Hong Kong. High-resolution Doppler LiDAR wind profiles are integrated with surface meteorological observations, ERA5 reanalysis data and urban morphology across multiple Local Climate Zones (LCZs). The Self-Organizing Map method (SOM) is used to classify hourly vertical wind profiles into four wind patterns. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) performs best among the tested models and is used to interpret the interactions between weather conditions and localized morphology. Thermal differences are found within the same LCZ types and vary under the vertical wind structure. Pattern 2 shows the weakest ventilation and strongest nocturnal stability with wind speed of 1.97 m s -1 at 50 m at the urban core site and boundary layer height of approximately 230 m. Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and building density have their greatest relative predictive importance under this pattern. Pattern 4 is associated with the deepest boundary layer and lowest nocturnal UHI among all patterns, although lower-level wind speeds at the urban site remain lower than those at the exposed site. Incorporating the structural variations of the atmospheric boundary layer into spatial assessments may provide a physical foundation for heat resilience and climate-sensitive design in urban planning.

title: Physics-informed AI-integrated digital twin framework for early and real-time prediction of mould growth in buildings
abstract: Indoor air quality issues, particularly mould and dampness, remain persistent public health concerns in residential buildings despite improvements in building standards and energy performance regulations. In current practice, mould management is largely reactive and relies on occupant complaints and visual inspection after mould has already become visible, at which occupants may have already experienced prolonged exposure to unhealthy indoor environment. To address this limitation, this study proposes a Digital Twin–based framework for continuous monitoring and predictive assessment of mould risk in buildings. The framework combines continuous environmental monitoring using an Internet of Things (IoT) sensor network with a calibrated Building Energy Model (BEM) that synchronizes real-time sensor data with simulation outputs to estimate surface hygrothermal condition across both monitored and unmonitored locations. These hygrothermal conditions are then used to evaluate mould development using the VTT mould growth model. Building upon this physics-based representation of mould dynamics, a Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) model based on Extreme Gradient Boosting is developed to forecast mould growth across prediction horizons ranging from 1 hour to 1 week. The proposed framework was implemented and validated on a sensor-instrumented residential building case study located in Syracuse, New York, achieving high prediction accuracy of up to R² of 0.99 for short-term forecasts and approximately 0.90 for longer horizons up to one-week-ahead mould index prediction. The findings demonstrate reliable prediction of mould development under dynamically changing indoor environment. The framework provides a scalable approach for real-time monitoring and proactive mould risk assessment in new and existing building to improve operation and add a new automated layer for maintenance, enabling early smart decision-making and intervention.

title: Large language model agents capture heterogeneous occupant behaviors in building energy simulation of shared office spaces
abstract: Occupant behavior is a major source of uncertainty in building energy simulation, yet existing models struggle to effectively capture the behavioral diversity within shared office spaces. Specifically, traditional probabilistic models fail to characterize individual differences, while large language model agents lack sufficient exploration in multi-occupant social contexts. To bridge this gap, this study couples physics-based building energy simulation with large language model agents to represent heterogeneous occupants with distinct thermal comfort preferences, psychological expectations, and energy-saving intentions. A closed-loop framework links environmental sensing, agent reasoning and control actions in real time. Tested through a four-person shared office scenario, the simulation successfully demonstrates the technical feasibility of this framework, which yields profile-dependent behavioral dynamics. Quantitative analysis reveals a highly concentrated distribution of operational authority, where one dominant occupant executed 62.1% of all control actions, whereas the least active occupant contributed only 1.3%. Within this simulated case, this study observes a sequential propagation chain from individual differences through group interactions and action execution to energy consumption feedback. Furthermore, the proposed framework provides a computational basis for investigating socially mediated occupant behavior in human-centric building operations.

Multi-field coupled optimization of an air-purifying BIPVT system with thermal–UV synergistic disinfection: A CFD–Bayesian optimization approach
abstract: The use of renewable energy to reduce building energy consumption has become a major trend, while indoor bioaerosol control has received increasing attention in the post-pandemic era. Air-purifying building-integrated photovoltaic/thermal (BIPVT) systems can provide power generation, space heating, and air purification without additional energy input, offering a pathway to integrate building energy efficiency with indoor health. In this study, a thermal–UV synergistic inactivation mechanism is introduced to enhance the bioaerosol control capability of such systems. However, the highly non-uniform temperature, UV radiation, and flow fields, together with multi-dimensional structural parameters, make the coordinated optimization of power generation, heating, and air purification challenging. To address this issue, Bayesian optimization is introduced for the first time into BIPVT system optimization through a coupled CFD–Bayesian optimization framework. The results show that: 1. Bayesian optimization rapidly identified high-value regions within the first 20 iterations and increased the optimal scalarized utility to 2.068, representing a 19% improvement. 2. Under equal weighting of heat gain, power generation, and air purification, high-value designs were mainly associated with moderate PV coverage and upper-channel UV lamp placement. 3. Compared with random and uniform sampling, Bayesian optimization achieved 5.1% and 15.6% higher optimal scalarized utilities under comparable sample sizes. 4. Parametric analysis further confirmed its stability and effectiveness under different UV wavelengths, channel depths, and lamp numbers, while increasing UV lamps showed limited marginal benefits beyond two lamps. The results provide insights for controlling indoor airborne disease and offer a new approach for optimizing BIPVT systems.

title: Air purifier performance in an occupied office: Field CADR and effectiveness from a reconstructed device-off condition
abstract: Air-purifier performance in an occupied building is hard to assess because the indoor concentration without the device cannot be observed under the same conditions. This study reconstructs that device-off condition from long-term field measurements in an occupied office. Two sequentially coupled physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), constrained by the CO 2 and PM 2.5 mass balances, estimate the time-varying air change rate, penetration factor and removal rate, and the removal rate is re-evaluated at each instant with the air-purifier input switched off. The difference between the two removal rates gives field CADR, and the modelled concentrations with the device on and off give steady-state and dynamic effectiveness. Field CADR is an equivalent removal rate specific to this room and device, not a chamber CADR. With the window and door closed, the median field CADR was 175 m 3 /h and the steady-state effectiveness was 0.79. With the window, the door or both open they fell to 50–66 m 3 /h and 0.09–0.31; the open-condition values are less precise, whereas the closed-open difference was reproduced in synthetic-data tests within the same model class. A conventional before/after comparison on the same record agreed with the reconstruction in the aggregate under the closed condition but not event by event, returned negative values under full opening, and yielded 59 estimates against 3613 from the proposed field CADR estimation. Its generality beyond one office remains to be established.
